::: {.solutions}

**Show all your reasoning.** Total: **34 marks** · Suggested time: **60 minutes**.

Every question here is harder than the eight TMUA questions on the
[T2 concepts page](t02_shapes_as_logic.qmd), and most are taken from other admissions papers. Close that
page before you start; the cards are what you are being tested on.

::: {.callout-important}
## What earns the marks

**Do not try to prove the false ones.** Reach for a **named shape**.

Every "not sufficient" or "not necessary" verdict wants a specific figure — *a kite that is not a rhombus*,
*a non-square rectangle*, *an isosceles trapezium* — together with the property that fails. A verdict with no
named figure scores the method mark at most.

Every **"if and only if"** claim needs **both directions** argued separately. Saying "they are the same thing"
earns nothing.
:::

|---|---|---|

# Section A — As set

## Question 1 **[3]** &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2023 · Q1H</span>

::: {.question}
Which of these triangles has the **largest area**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** an isosceles triangle with side lengths $10,10,1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** an isosceles triangle with side lengths $10,10,5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** an isosceles triangle with side lengths $10,10,10$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** an isosceles triangle with side lengths $10,10,15$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(e)** an isosceles triangle with side lengths $10,10,19$

Give the letter, **and** say what the largest possible area of a triangle with two sides of length $10$ is,
and which triangle achieves it. **[3]**
:::

## Question 2 **[8]** &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q20</span>

::: {.question}
**Statement $P$:** $ABC$ is a right-angled triangle.

Which of the following statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** $P$ is true **if and only if** triangle $ABC$ can be divided by a line segment into two
smaller triangles, each of which is similar to triangle $ABC$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** $P$ is **necessary** for triangle $ABC$ to be divisible by a line segment into two
smaller triangles whose areas, together with the area of $ABC$, can be arranged to form a geometric sequence
with common ratio not equal to $1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** $P$ is a **necessary** condition that must be satisfied by all the triangles made when a
convex kite is divided into four triangles by its diagonals.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** $P$ is **sufficient** for triangle $ABC$ to be determined uniquely up to congruence by
the length of its hypotenuse and the length of the median to its hypotenuse.
*(The median to the hypotenuse joins the opposite vertex to the midpoint of the hypotenuse.)*

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** $P$ is true **if and only if** four congruent copies of triangle $ABC$ can be assembled
edge-to-edge, without gaps or overlaps, so that their union is exactly a rhombus.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** (1), (3), (5) only &nbsp;&nbsp;**B** (3), (5) only &nbsp;&nbsp;**C** (1), (2), (3), (5) only
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** (1), (5) only &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** (1), (3), (4), (5) only &nbsp;&nbsp;**F** (1), (3) only

Give the letter, and **one line of justification for every one of the five statements** — a proof sketch for
each true one, a specific figure for each false one. **[8]**
:::

# Section B — The midpoint quadrilateral

## Question 3 **[10]**

::: {.question}
Let $ABCD$ be any convex quadrilateral, and let $E$, $F$, $G$, $H$ be the midpoints of $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DA$
respectively.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Using vectors, show that $EFGH$ is **always** a parallelogram, whatever $ABCD$ is, and
that its sides are parallel to the diagonals of $ABCD$ and half their length. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Hence prove that $EFGH$ is a **rhombus** if and only if the diagonals of $ABCD$ are
equal in length. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** Prove that $EFGH$ is a **rectangle** if and only if the diagonals of $ABCD$ are
perpendicular. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** State, with a one-line reason, the condition on the diagonals of $ABCD$ that makes
$EFGH$ a **square**. Then give a specific $ABCD$ which is **not** a square but whose $EFGH$ is. **[2]**
:::

:::

# Section C — Deductions and constructions

## Question 4 **[4]**

::: {.question}
In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A=30^\circ$, $AB=x^{2}$ and $BC=2x$, where $x>0$. There are exactly **two
non-congruent** triangles satisfying these conditions.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Find the exact set of values of $x$. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Which **one** of the following can therefore be *deduced*? Explain in one sentence why
the others cannot, even though some of them overlap your answer to (a). **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1<x<5$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $2<x<3$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $3<x<5$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $0<x<3$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $x>3$
:::

## Question 5 **[4]**

::: {.question}
Prove that in **any** right-angled triangle, the median to the hypotenuse has length exactly half the
hypotenuse. **[2]**

Hence explain why knowing *both* the hypotenuse and that median does **not** determine a right-angled
triangle up to congruence, and give two non-congruent right-angled triangles with hypotenuse $10$ to show
it. **[2]**
:::

## Question 6 **[5]**

::: {.question}
A rhombus has side length $2$ and acute angle $60^\circ$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** Join the midpoints of one pair of opposite sides, then cut each of the two resulting
pieces along its longer diagonal. Show that this produces **four congruent triangles** that fill the rhombus
exactly, and find the three side lengths of one of them. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** Show that this triangle is **not** right-angled, and say which statement of Question 2
your construction has just disproved. **[2]**
:::

## Before you hand this in

2. Every **"if and only if"** in Question 3 has **two** arguments, one per direction.
3. In Question 4 you wrote down the exact range **first**, and only then went looking among the options.
4. Wherever you recovered an angle from a sine, you considered **both** $\theta$ and $180^\circ-\theta$.
